subject: Climate & Environment
title: Geothermal Energy
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Geothermal Energy.

hook.text: Drill deep enough anywhere on Earth and you will hit rock hot enough to boil water.

buildup.text: Iceland uses geothermal heat to warm 90% of its homes and generate a third of its power.

discovery.text: Steam from underground reservoirs spins turbines just like coal or gas — minus the emissions.

twist.text: New drilling technology could unlock geothermal almost anywhere, not just volcanic zones.

climax.text: Enhanced geothermal systems inject water into hot rock and harvest the resulting steam.

punchline.text: The biggest power plant is the one under our feet.

quiz.question: What percentage of Iceland's homes are heated with geothermal energy?

details.summary: Geothermal energy taps heat from within the Earth to produce electricity and direct heating. Conventional plants use naturally occurring steam or hot water near tectonic boundaries.
details.whyItMatters: Geothermal provides constant baseload power regardless of weather, complementing intermittent solar and wind. Enhanced systems could make it available globally, not just along fault lines.
takeaways: Geothermal plants use Earth's internal heat for power
Conventional plants need natural steam near tectonic boundaries
Enhanced systems could unlock geothermal energy everywhere

faq.question: Where is geothermal energy most available?
faq.answer: Conventional geothermal is concentrated along tectonic plate boundaries: Iceland, the western US, East Africa, Indonesia, and the Philippines. Enhanced geothermal systems aim to access hot rock at depth practically anywhere, greatly expanding the resource.

faq.question: Is geothermal energy truly clean?
faq.answer: Geothermal emits very low CO2 compared to fossil fuels, typically 10 to 20 times less per kilowatt-hour. Some plants release trace hydrogen sulfide. Closed-loop systems further reduce emissions. Water use and induced seismicity are manageable concerns.
